Content Writer Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A content writer resume faces a unique test: it's judged on how well it demonstrates the very skill it's selling. Hiring managers — content leads, marketing directors, editors — read your bullets the way they read a draft: hunting for clarity, specificity, and evidence you understand how writing drives business outcomes, not just words on a page.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, a section-by-section breakdown, the skills and keywords hiring managers search for, and the mistakes that quietly cost interviews.

Quick answer: A content writer resume should include a niche-focused summary with output and proof (e.g. 120+ articles, 340K sessions), quantified experience bullets pairing formats with results, a skills section naming SEO tools and CMS platforms exactly, a prominent portfolio link, and keywords mirrored from the job posting. Metrics are what get the interview.

Key Takeaways

  • Your resume is the writing sample — every bullet must demonstrate the clarity, specificity, and evidence the job demands.
  • Pair formats with metrics: traffic grown, rankings won, pipeline influenced. Numbers get interviews; duties don't.
  • Name SEO tools, CMS platforms, and analytics exactly — they are literal ATS filters on content job postings.
  • Put the portfolio link in the header, not the footer, and keep your three best pieces one click away.
  • Mirror the posting's language and run your finished resume through Cvyon's free ATS grader before you apply.

What Content Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask a content lead what separates a good writer from a hireable one and you won't hear “great storyteller.” You'll hear:

  • Proof your writing performed. Traffic growth, rankings, conversions, engagement — the metrics tied to what you published. A resume with no numbers reads like a writer who's never been measured.
  • Range with a specialty. Blog posts, landing pages, case studies, email sequences, white papers — hiring managers want breadth, but they hire for the format they need filled. Name your strongest formats explicitly.
  • SEO and distribution literacy. Most content exists to be found. Keyword research, search intent, internal linking, content refreshes — these are hiring filters, not nice-to-haves, for most content roles.
  • Process and volume. Editorial calendars, briefs, style guides, stakeholder management. Can you ship 8 articles a month without chaos? Show the system, not just the sentences.
  • Subject-matter depth. B2B SaaS, fintech, health, legal — writers who already speak the industry's language get hired faster. Your portfolio and bullets should prove domain fluency.

If your resume reads like a list of places you wrote, it will lose to one that reads like a record of what your writing did.

Content Writer Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is a complete example for a B2B SaaS content writer. It's fictional — the names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern real hiring managers respond to: what you wrote, the scale, and the result.

PRIYA NAIR
Chicago, IL · (312) 555-0163 · priya.nair@email.com · Portfolio: priyanairwrites.com

SUMMARY
Content writer with 5 years producing B2B SaaS content. Published 120+ long-form articles driving 340K annual organic sessions; 14 articles rank in Google's top 3 for target keywords. Skilled in SEO content strategy, case studies, and email nurture sequences. Comfortable owning a topic from brief to publish to refresh.

SKILLS
Long-form blog writing · SEO content strategy · Keyword research (Ahrefs, Semrush) · Search intent mapping · Content refreshes & updates · Case studies & white papers · Landing page copy · Email nurture sequences · Editorial calendars · Style guides · Interviewing subject-matter experts · CMS publishing (WordPress, Webflow) · Analytics (GA4, Search Console)

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Content Writer — Northbeam Analytics (B2B SaaS), Chicago, IL | 2021–Present

  • Own the company blog end to end: 8 articles per month from brief through publish, maintaining a 98% on-time rate across 3 years
  • Grew organic blog traffic from 90K to 340K annual sessions by building a 60-article topic cluster around the product's core use cases
  • Ranked 14 articles in Google's top 3 for commercial-intent keywords, contributing to 22% of marketing-sourced pipeline
  • Interviewed 25+ customers and turned calls into 12 published case studies; 3 are now top-10 pages on the site
  • Run quarterly content refreshes on the top 40 pages, recovering an average 18% traffic lift per refreshed article

Staff Writer — The Loop (digital media), Remote | 2019–2021

  • Wrote 200+ consumer-tech articles and buying guides under daily deadlines; 3 guides held #1 rankings for 12+ months
  • Adapted to 4 editorial style guides; copyedited 15 freelancer submissions per month

EDUCATION
B.A., English — University of Illinois Chicago, 2019

CERTIFICATIONS
HubSpot Content Marketing Certification — 2022

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: name the niche, the output, and the proof

“Niche” is doing heavy lifting here — “B2B SaaS content” tells the hiring manager you're already fluent in their world. The output (120+ articles) proves volume; the proof (340K sessions, 14 top-3 rankings) proves performance. If you're earlier in your career, swap the traffic numbers for range: “40 published pieces across blog, email, and landing pages.”

Experience: attach metrics to formats

Each bullet should pair a format with a result. “Grew organic blog traffic from 90K to 340K” is the anchor; “22% of marketing-sourced pipeline” connects writing to revenue — the sentence that gets you the interview. Even junior writers can measure something: pieces published, deadlines hit, pages refreshed, interviews conducted. “Maintaining a 98% on-time rate” matters because content leads live in fear of the bottleneck writer.

Freelance and contract work counts fully. List clients or “select clients” the same way — with formats and results, not just names.

Skills: group by what hiring managers search

Content job posts are keyword-dense, and applicant tracking systems screen for exact terms. Group your skills so a scanner finds them fast: SEO tools named explicitly (Ahrefs, Semrush), CMS platforms (WordPress, Webflow), analytics (GA4, Search Console). These tool names are often the literal ATS filters.

Portfolio link: non-negotiable

The example puts the portfolio URL in the header, not buried in a bullet. For writers, the portfolio IS the resume's proof section. Link it prominently, keep it current, and make sure the 3 best pieces are reachable in one click. A dead portfolio link is worse than none — verify it before every application.

Content Writer Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the job posting's language exactly — “SEO content” vs “search-optimized writing” — and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Writing & editing: long-form articles, blog writing, copyediting, proofreading, headline writing, tone-of-voice adaptation, style guides (AP, Chicago), fact-checking
  • SEO & distribution: keyword research, search intent, on-page SEO, internal linking, content clusters, meta descriptions, content refreshes, SERP analysis, featured snippets
  • Formats: case studies, white papers, ebooks, landing pages, email sequences, newsletters, scripts, social copy, product descriptions, buying guides
  • Tools: Ahrefs, Semrush, Clearscope, Surfer, WordPress, Webflow, Google Docs, GA4, Google Search Console, Grammarly, Hemingway
  • Process: editorial calendars, content briefs, stakeholder interviews, SME collaboration, freelance management, publishing workflows, content audits

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Writers lose interviews to parsing failures more often than they'd believe: multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual killers. Start from a clean template like the ones at Cvyon's content-writer page or the template gallery.

5 Mistakes That Cost Content Interviews

  1. No metrics anywhere. “Wrote blog posts” is a duty, not a result. Even one number — articles per month, traffic lift, rankings — changes how the resume reads.
  2. Hiding the portfolio. Buried in a footer link or missing entirely. For writers, the portfolio belongs in the header, right under your name.
  3. Generic “excellent written communication.” Every applicant claims it; none prove it. Delete the phrase and let a sharp bullet prove it instead.
  4. Ignoring SEO vocabulary. If the job post says “search intent” and your resume says nothing about SEO, the ATS may never pass you to a human. Mirror the posting's terms.
  5. A wall of text. Writers who can't format a one-page resume raise doubts about their editorial judgment. White space, scannable bullets, one idea per line.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a content writer resume?

A niche-focused summary with output and proof (e.g. 120+ articles, 340K sessions); quantified experience bullets pairing formats with results; a skills section naming SEO tools (Ahrefs, Semrush), CMS platforms (WordPress, Webflow), and analytics (GA4, Search Console) exactly; a prominent portfolio link in the header; and keywords mirrored from the job posting. Metrics are what get the interview.

How long should a content writer resume be?

One page, almost always. Content leads skim dozens of applications; a tight page demonstrates the editing judgment the job requires. Two pages only with 8+ years and genuinely distinct roles.

Do I need SEO skills to get hired as a content writer?

For most content marketing roles, yes — it’s a baseline expectation now, not a specialty. You don’t need to be a technical SEO, but keyword research, search intent, and on-page basics should be on the resume. Pure editorial roles (magazines, books) are the exception.

Should I include freelance writing on my resume?

Absolutely — list it as a role with the same format-and-result bullets as staff jobs. “Freelance Content Writer — 40+ articles for 12 B2B clients, 2022–2024” with two metric-bearing bullets beats a gap every time.

What if I don’t have traffic metrics to show?

Use what you can measure: pieces published, deadlines hit, formats covered, interviews conducted, pages refreshed. And start measuring now — even GA4 access on a personal blog gives you real numbers within months.

Should my resume link to social media?

Only if it demonstrates writing: a LinkedIn with published articles, a Substack, a Medium with real readership. A personal Instagram adds nothing for most content roles. The portfolio link is what matters.
